about: Explainer clips the hint player, data cards and Journal play (MASTER_PLAN.md section 5). Science explainers are built by production/tools/motion/build.py from production/explainers/motion/specs/; do not edit their entries by hand.

explainers.title: Moving and looking

captions.text: Walk with W, A, S and D, or the left stick.
A and D step sideways. S walks back.
To look around, hold the right mouse button and move, or use the right stick.
Head for the gold outline. Walking never runs down a hidden clock.

explainers.ends_on: Head for the gold outline. Walking never runs down a hidden clock.

explainers.title: Why cold traps hold ice

captions.text: Near the pole, the Sun stays so low that some crater floors never see it.
Those floors sit in shadow all year, every year.
In that dark, Shackleton's floor is colder than −183 °C.
One cold trap measured by NASA's Diviner is about −235 °C.
Ice that drifts in there stays frozen for a very long time.
That number is an estimate for one spot.

explainers.ends_on: The coldest places keep ice, but they are also the hardest places to work.

explainers.title: Cotton on the Moon

captions.text: In 2019, China's Chang'e-4 lander carried seeds to the Moon's far side.
Inside a small sealed can, a cotton seed sprouted into a green seedling.
So a seed can sprout on the Moon, inside a sealed can.
But it never flowered or made seeds.
That was one small, sealed experiment.

explainers.ends_on: A sprout is a start, not a harvest. Growing food on the Moon still has to be proven.

explainers.title: Air, water and food for a crew

captions.text: Every day, one astronaut needs three things: air, water and food.
About 0.9 kg of oxygen to breathe.
About 3.2 kg of water to drink, and 0.8 kg of food.
And they breathe out about 1.1 kg of carbon dioxide.
A crew of four needs four times as much, every single day.
Without any one of the three, the crew cannot stay.
These are planning values for an average adult.

explainers.ends_on: Each shift uses a little of everything. Keep a margin, so one bad night cannot run you out.

explainers.title: Where is Earth from the pole?

captions.text: From the south pole, Earth never climbs high. It hugs the horizon.
Through April 2046 it rocks slowly up above the edge, then down below it.
From 15 April to 28 April, Earth is below the horizon: no direct radio link.
Chapter 1's night falls inside that gap.
On the best peak near the pole, Earth is in view 51% of the time.
The same peak gets sunlight 92% of the time.
That is why relay stations go on high peaks.
So in the game, shift 4's link cutoff is a training drill.

explainers.ends_on: When Earth is out of view, no one can answer quickly. Your crew plans and decides on its own.

explainers.title: Impact flashes

captions.text: Tiny bits of space rock hit the Moon and make brief flashes of light.
NASA watches the Moon's dark side for them about 10 nights a month.
In the first five years they confirmed 126 flashes, 62% during meteor showers.
A camera can glitch, so one sighting is not enough.
A flash counts only when two telescopes both see it at the same moment.
These flashes were watched from Earth.

explainers.ends_on: Trust a reading when two independent checks agree, not when one says so.

explainers.title: Mapping the Moon with a laser

captions.text: NASA's LRO spacecraft fires laser pulses at the Moon from orbit.
Timing each echo gives the distance, and so the height of the ground.
Millions of those heights make a map, down to one point every 5 m.
This is the real ridge where Aurora stands.
Two NASA maps of it agree to about 1.4 m.
From heights you get slopes: how steep each step is.
So the road to the cold trap is 8.6 km, never steeper than 12°.

explainers.ends_on: Real maps make real plans. Check the slope on the map before you drive.

explainers.title: The long road to Malapert

captions.text: Places on the Moon have official names, kept on a public map.
Mons Malapert is a real mountain about 122 km from the south pole.
That is almost three marathons laid end to end.
But a rover cannot drive straight over craters and steep slopes.
A road on gentle ground is about 198 km long.
Those are the features' centres.

explainers.ends_on: The straight line is never the road. Pack for the road you will actually drive.

explainers.title: Low gravity

captions.text: On the Moon you weigh about one-sixth of what you weigh on Earth.
So every step becomes a bound, and you float down slowly.
With no air, kicked-up dust flies in clean arcs and drops straight back.
Less weight on the wheels means less grip, so stopping takes longer.

explainers.ends_on: Move slower than feels natural, and leave yourself room to stop.

explainers.title: Moonquakes

captions.text: Apollo astronauts left seismometers on the Moon, and the ground moved.
From 1971 to 1976 they recorded 28 shallow moonquakes.
The strongest reached magnitude 3.2: enough to rattle a base.
A quake shakes anything that is not held down.
That is why equipment on the Moon is strapped and latched.
These were recorded far from the south pole.

explainers.ends_on: Before the ground shakes, latch what matters. Loose things fall.

explainers.title: How plants grow in space

captions.text: Fast Plants can go from seed to new seeds in about 40 days.
They flower after about 14 days.
Then pollen must travel from one plant to another; they cannot pollinate themselves.
About 20 days later, the seeds are ripe.
On the Mir space station, Brassica plants grew from seed to seed.
Astronauts moved the pollen by hand, flower to flower.
On the ISS, Brassica greens grew under lamps for 27 days.
Those plants grew in orbit, not on the Moon.

explainers.ends_on: A seed needs light, time and a partner plant. Plan for all three.

explainers.title: Why the Sun stays low at the pole

captions.text: The Moon spins standing almost straight up, like a top.
So at the south pole, sunlight comes in from the side.
The Sun never climbs. It rolls around the edge of the sky.
Here is how high the Sun gets in 2046 and 2047. Zero is the horizon.
It stays between −1.56° and +1.59°: just a peek above or below.
That is smaller than your thumb held out at arm's length!
So up high is best. A tall crater rim can stay sunny 240 days straight.
Down in the crater it stays dark. Even on the rim, darkness can last 1.5 days.

explainers.ends_on: Sunlight here comes and goes. In the dark shifts, the base runs on its battery alone.

explainers.title: Reading a proton-flux chart

captions.text: A weather satellite near Earth counts tiny, fast bits of the Sun: protons.
Its count is in pfu: protons per square centimetre, each second.
On a normal scale, a quiet day is so small you cannot even see it.
On a log scale, each step up is ten times bigger. Now both fit!
10 September 2017: an X8.2 flare bursts on the Sun at 15:35 UTC.
At 16:45 UTC, the protons cross the storm line: 10 pfu.
That is just seventy minutes after the flare began.
Then they stay high for days, peaking at 1,493.5 pfu!
The Moon has no air or magnetic shield, so storms like this reach the ground.

explainers.ends_on: When the alarm sounds, the protons are already on their way. Get the shelter ready before it!

explainers.title: The red ring

captions.text: On 12 January 2047, the Sun, Earth and Moon line up.
The Moon slides into Earth's shadow: a total lunar eclipse.
From the Moon, Earth covers the whole Sun.
Sunlight bending through Earth's air paints a thin red ring around it.
The full shadow lasts about 70 minutes.
Those minutes are for the whole Moon.

explainers.ends_on: While Earth hides the Sun, the panels make almost nothing. Plan the battery for the dark.

explainers.title: Relays and line of sight

captions.text: Radio travels in straight lines, and the Moon's surface curves away.
Around 8 April 2047, Earth is below the pole's horizon: no direct link.
A relay on a high peak can see both the base and Earth.
To see Earth then, it must stand at least 1.4 km high.
Repeaters along a road pass the signal hop by hop.
This is geometry, before the real terrain check.

explainers.ends_on: If you cannot see it, you cannot talk to it. Put a relay where both ends are in view.

explainers.title: Rovers and slopes

captions.text: Lunar dust is loose, so steep slopes make rover wheels slip.
NASA's VIPER rover was designed to climb slopes up to 15°.
Any steeper, and it has to find another way around.
On a map, the shortest line can be the steepest.
A longer, gentler route is often the safe one.
That limit is VIPER's design figure.

explainers.ends_on: Check the slope before you drive. The short way is not always the safe way.

explainers.title: What shielding does

captions.text: Fast protons lose energy as they push through anything in their way.
Water is great at this, because it is packed with light hydrogen atoms.
The thicker the wall, the fewer get through.
A model of a huge 1972 solar storm shows what thicker shielding does.
Behind the thinnest wall, about 185 mSv. Behind the thickest, about 85.
Thicker walls cut the dose, but it never drops to zero.
So crews do three things: put shielding up, get behind it fast, and stay there.

explainers.ends_on: Every layer of water helps, but only if it is in place before the protons arrive.

explainers.title: Solar power and batteries

captions.text: Near the pole the Sun stays low, so solar panels stand tall and upright.
This NASA design hangs a 10 kW panel from a 16 m mast.
It turns to keep facing the Sun.
A battery works like a water tank: sunlight fills it, the base drains it.
When the tank is full, any extra power spills away and is lost.
So spare power is best used while you have it.
When the Sun hides, nothing flows in. The base lives on the tank.
If the tank runs dry, the lights and heaters go dark.

explainers.ends_on: Use spare power before it spills, and keep enough in the tank for the dark.

explainers.title: Solar storms in 2012 and 2017

captions.text: In July 2012, the Sun threw out a huge cloud at about 3,435 km/s.
It missed Earth and hit the STEREO-A spacecraft instead.
STEREO-A's protons rose within hours; the shock arrived about 17 hours later.
The 2017 storm did reach Earth, peaking near 1,494 pfu.
Both are real. Only one hit home.
So the game's storm asks: what if the 2012 storm had hit the Moon?

explainers.ends_on: Real storms set the rules. Prepare as if the big one is aimed at you.

explainers.title: How we know there is water

captions.text: On 9 October 2009, NASA crashed a spent rocket stage into a dark crater.
A second spacecraft flew through the plume and measured it.
About 5.6% of it was water ice, give or take 2.9%.
Another instrument looked for ice right at the surface.
It found exposed ice in only 3.5% of the cold traps.
So ice is patchy.
Some places hold plenty, most hold little, and none of it is ready to drink.

explainers.ends_on: Test before you trust: one sample does not tell you the whole crater.
